true_positives.matched_candidate:
Script uses BSD-only sed syntax and cwd-relative paths

`sed -i '' -E` is macOS/BSD syntax. On GNU sed (Linux), `''` is treated as the script argument and the command fails, so the env file isn't updated. `ENV_FILE="../.env"` is resolved against the current working directory rather than the script's location, so running it from the repo root writes outside the repo. Also, `cleanup` always exits 0, even on the rate-limit and failed-to-extract-URL paths, so callers can't detect these failures.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Plain Error thrown instead of TRPCError

When the credential isn't found or isn't owned by the user, the handler throws a generic `Error`. tRPC reports this as INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (500), and the error gets logged/alerted as a server fault. Throw `new TRPCError({ code: "NOT_FOUND" })` (or FORBIDDEN) so clients get a proper status and monitoring isn't polluted.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Timestamp formatted with hardcoded en-US locale

The cache timestamp is formatted with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)`, ignoring the user's locale from `useLocale` and their time format preference. Non-US users will see M/D/YY dates, which is ambiguous next to otherwise translated strings.

false_positives.candidate:
Backfill sets all legacy rows' updatedAt to migration time

The column is added with `DEFAULT NOW()`, so every existing cache row gets the migration timestamp as its `updatedAt`. Until each row is rewritten, the new UI will show a fresh "Last updated" time for potentially very stale cache. A more accurate backfill, e.g. `expiresAt - interval '30 days'` (the caching TTL), would avoid misleading users.

Cache deletion does not invalidate connectedCalendars query

The `deleteCache` mutation's `onSuccess` only shows a toast and calls the optional `onSuccess` prop. It never invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`, which the disconnect mutation does. In `SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper`, `onChanged` is often undefined, and the query uses `refetchOnWindowFocus: false`. As a result, after deleting the cache the dropdown keeps showing the old "Cache Status / Last updated" entry and the delete action until a full reload. Users are told it succeeded while the UI still shows cached data.

Cache status includes expired entries

`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups all `CalendarCache` rows by credential without filtering on `expiresAt >= now`. Expired rows are never served by `getCachedAvailability`, yet they still make the UI report a cache with a "Last updated" timestamp. This is misleading about whether cached data is actually in use. Add `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }` to the where clause.

UserWithCalendars now requires updatedAt and googleChannelId

`allSelectedCalendars` and `userLevelSelectedCalendars` now require `updatedAt` and `googleChannelId`. Only `findUnlockedUserForSession` was updated to select these fields. Any other caller of `getConnectedDestinationCalendarsAndEnsureDefaultsInDb`, such as the platform API through the legacy export, will hit type errors if its user object doesn't select them. Nothing in this PR uses these fields, so the type widening appears unnecessary.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder cancellation is fire-and-forget and may never run

`deleteScheduledEmailReminder` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are called inside `forEach` without awaiting them. Before this change the DB deletes were collected and awaited; now the `cancelled: true` update and the SMS cancel/delete run detached from the request.

On serverless deployments, execution can be frozen or killed once the response is returned. In that case the `cancelled` flag is never written, and the reminder email is still sent, which is the bug this PR is meant to fix.

The same pattern appears in bookings.tsx (requestReschedule) and workflows.tsx. Collect the promises and await them.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reschedule still cancels SendGrid sends immediately, hitting the same 100-cancellation limit

When a booking is rescheduled, every email reminder of the original booking is passed to `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(..., true)`. That calls SendGrid `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` with status `cancel` right away. Workflow deletion (workflows.tsx line 214) and step deletion (line 521) take the same immediate path.

The PR says the root cause was that SendGrid allows at most 100 pending cancellations, so they should be deferred until shortly before send time. Rescheduling is a frequent action and each one adds pending cancellations again. Once the limit is reached, cancellations fail silently (the error is only logged) and emails for rescheduled bookings go out again.

Also, the immediate path returns without deleting or flagging the `WorkflowReminder` row, so the DB keeps a stale `scheduled: true` reminder for the old booking. Rescheduling should use the deferred `cancelled` flag like the cancel path does.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Deferred cancellation misses reminders due before the next cron run

Cancellation now only happens in this cron, which runs every 15 minutes. It cancels reminders whose `scheduledDate` is within the next hour.

If a booking is cancelled when its reminder is less than about 15 minutes from its send time, the cron may not run before SendGrid sends it. Worse, the `deleteMany` above removes rows whose `scheduledDate` has passed, so the reminder is dropped without ever being cancelled.

When the scheduled date is close (for example within 1–2 hours), `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` should cancel immediately instead of only setting the flag.

One failing SendGrid cancel aborts the batch and leaves already-cancelled reminders undeleted

The try/catch wraps the whole loop. If any `client.request` throws, the loop stops, and `Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete)` is never reached.

Prisma queries are lazy and only run when awaited. So the deletes for reminders that were already cancelled at SendGrid in this run never execute. Those reminders stay `cancelled: true` and are cancelled again on every cron run, which can keep failing (for example on a duplicate cancel or an invalid batch). Every reminder after the failing one is never cancelled, so those emails are sent.

Handle errors per reminder and delete each reminder once its cancel succeeds.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
try/catch around forEach(async) no longer catches errors

The callback was made `async` so it can `await getCalendar(...)`. `forEach` ignores the returned promises, so the surrounding try/catch cannot catch failures from `getCalendar`, `deleteEvent` or `deleteMeeting`. Before this change, synchronous failures in `getCalendar` were caught and logged.

Now those failures become unhandled promise rejections, and the calendar/video deletions are fire-and-forget. The function returns and sends emails before deletions finish.

Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` inside the try.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
try/catch around forEach(async) no longer catches errors

The callback was made `async` so it can `await getCalendar(...)`. `forEach` ignores the returned promises, so the surrounding try/catch cannot catch failures from `getCalendar`, `deleteEvent` or `deleteMeeting`. Before this change, synchronous failures in `getCalendar` were caught and logged.

Now those failures become unhandled promise rejections, and the calendar/video deletions are fire-and-forget. The function returns and sends emails before deletions finish.

Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` inside the try.

false_positives.candidate:
Fire-and-forget async forEach in requestReschedule

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...)` now awaits `getCalendar` inside each callback, but the promises are never awaited or handled.

Any rejection from `getCalendar`, `deleteEvent` or `deleteMeeting` becomes an unhandled rejection in the tRPC server. The mutation also proceeds to send emails and webhooks without knowing whether the old events were deleted.

Await `Promise.all` over a `map` and handle errors.

Recurring deletes pushed to apiDeletes after it is awaited

Inside `forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(...) })`, each push happens only after at least one microtask.

The outer handler later runs `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` (and `await apiDeletes` on the paid path). By then these pushes have usually not happened, so recurring calendar deletions are not awaited and their errors go unhandled. The new `await getCalendar` makes this ordering race certain.

Use a `for...of` loop, as was done for the non-credentialId branch.

getCalendarCredentials now returns `calendar` as a Promise and eagerly starts work

`getCalendar` is now async, so `calendar` in each returned item is a `Promise<Calendar | null>`, not a `Calendar`.

`getConnectedCalendars` was updated to await it. Any other consumer of `getCalendarCredentials` / `ReturnType<typeof getCalendarCredentials>` that uses `item.calendar` directly will now call methods on a Promise and break at runtime. This includes API routes and tRPC handlers that list calendars.

Also, these promises are created for every credential up front. If one rejects and the consumer never awaits it, the result is an unhandled rejection.

Either keep the field lazy (store a function) or audit and update all consumers.

try/catch around forEach(async) no longer catches errors

Same issue as in the vital reschedule. The async callback's promise is dropped by `forEach`, so errors from `await getCalendar(...)` and the deletion calls escape the try/catch as unhandled rejections. The deletions also do not complete before the function returns.

Use `await Promise.all(...map(async ...))`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Slot end computed from slot start in working-hours check

`end` is computed as `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()`, which is identical to `start`. It should use `slotEndTime`. As written, a slot that starts inside working hours but runs past the end of them passes the check, so the end-of-day boundary is never enforced.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs objects compared with === so the empty-override case never matches

`dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)` compares two freshly created object references, so it is always false. A zero-length date override (the way a fixed host marks a whole day unavailable) is therefore never detected as fully blocking. A slot overlapping that instant falls through and is treated as available. Use `.isSame()` or compare `valueOf()`.

false_positives.candidate:
Offset-shifted override times wrap at midnight and are matched to the wrong day

After applying `offset`, only `hour()`/`minute()` are used, so a shifted override that crosses midnight wraps around. For example, 20:00–23:00 shifted by +3h becomes 23:00–02:00, i.e. startTime 1380 and endTime 120. `buildSlots` skips it because start >= end, so the override vanishes.

Separately, `activeOverrides` (line 207) selects overrides using the unshifted `override.start`. An override that moves into the next or previous invitee day after the offset is still applied to the original day.

Override containment check misses slots extending past override end and slots starting exactly at end

A slot is rejected only if it ends at or before the override start, or starts strictly after the override end.

- A slot starting exactly at the override end passes, because `isAfter` is false when the times are equal.
- A slot that starts inside the override but ends after it also passes.

In round-robin, slots are generated from all hosts' availability. So a fixed host can be booked partly or wholly outside their date override, which is the bug this PR set out to fix. The check should require `slotStart >= overrideStart && slotEnd <= overrideEnd`.

Override day matching mixes timezones and is UTC-date based

The override's day is taken from `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset).format(...)`, which formats in the server's local timezone. The slot's day comes from `slotStartTime.format(...)`, which is in UTC. On non-UTC servers these can disagree.

Matching on UTC dates is also problematic. For organizers far from UTC, an override on local day D can start on UTC day D-1. When that happens:

- Regular slots on UTC day D-1 outside the override are wrongly rejected.
- Day D falls back to normal working hours, ignoring the override.

Working-hours check rejects valid slots when a day has multiple working-hour ranges

`workingHours.find(...)` returns true as soon as any single working-hour entry for that weekday does not contain the slot, and the slot is then rejected. Take a schedule with split hours on one day, e.g. 9–12 and 13–17. A 14:00 slot is outside 9–12, so it is marked unavailable even though it falls inside 13–17. The same happens when one range is split across UTC days.

This check now runs for every fixed host, which includes all users of personal and collective events. Legitimate availability will disappear from booking pages. The check should require that the slot is contained in at least one range (`some` contains), not reject on the first range that doesn't contain it.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError when Integration metadata has no 'sender'

`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes every existing Integration has a `sender` entry. `build_integration` only sets `sender` when `state.get("sender")` is present, and integrations created before this field existed (or through other paths) will not have it.

For those integrations this line raises `KeyError`, and the user gets a 500 instead of the error page. Use `.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and fail gracefully with `error(...)`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
OAuth authorize URL parameters are not URL-encoded

The authorize URL is built with an f-string that puts `client_id`, `state` and `redirect_uri` in without encoding. `redirect_uri` is an absolute URL containing `:` and `/`, and on some deployments it could contain `?`, `&` or other characters that break the query string.

Build the query with `urlencode({...})` so the redirect URI is always encoded correctly.

OAuth state compared with non-constant-time equality

The `state` CSRF token is compared to `pipeline.signature` with `!=`, which is not a constant-time comparison. The practical risk is low, but security token comparisons should use `constant_time_compare` (or `hmac.compare_digest`) to avoid timing side channels.

Unhandled exceptions from token exchange / user lookup cause 500s

`safe_urlopen(...)` sits outside the try block, so network or SSL errors propagate unhandled. `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` raises (e.g. `IdentityNotValid`/`ApiError`) when GitHub rejects the token, and that is not caught either.

The PR description says these failure cases should render the "Invalid installation request" page. Instead they surface as server errors. Wrap both calls and return `error(request, self.active_organization)` on failure.

User-ownership check skipped when no Integration row exists for the installation_id

When `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `DoesNotExist`, the view calls `pipeline.next_step()` straight away. The new `github_authenticated_user` vs. installer check never runs on this path.

`build_integration` then fetches the installation with the app JWT and creates the Integration for whatever `installation_id` was supplied in the query string. An attacker can therefore claim any GitHub installation of the app that has no Integration row yet. Examples:
- an installation whose webhook has not been processed yet (a race);
- an installation whose Sentry Integration was deleted while the app stayed installed on GitHub.

The security validation only covers the case where the webhook already created the row. The installer/permission check should also run on this path, e.g. by verifying the authenticated user can access the installation via `GET /user/installations` with the OAuth token.

test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the 404 path

The test now sends a deliberately wrong `state` (`ddd023...`), so it only checks the state-mismatch error from `OAuthLoginView`. It never reaches `build_integration`'s 404 handling ("The GitHub installation could not be found.").

Coverage for the installation-not-found behavior is silently lost. Use the correct state so the flow reaches the 404 branch, and keep the original assertion.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`queued` default is evaluated once at import time

`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a plain default value. Python evaluates it once, when the class is defined at module import. Every `AssignmentSource` created afterwards (e.g. via `from_integration`) carries the same timestamp: the moment the worker process started, not when the assignment was queued.

Any later logic or debugging that relies on `queued` will be wrong, often by hours or days. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Task kwargs contain a raw datetime that won't survive JSON serialization

`assignment_source.to_dict()` uses `dataclasses.asdict`, so the `queued` field stays a `datetime` object. That dict is passed straight into `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs=...)`.

Sentry's task kwargs are expected to be JSON-serializable. A raw `datetime` either fails or triggers serialization warnings/errors. If it is coerced to a string, `from_dict` rebuilds the dataclass with `queued` as a `str`, silently breaking the declared type.

This matters most on the inbound-webhook path, which is the exact path the PR is meant to protect. Serialize `queued` explicitly (e.g. `isoformat()` or a timestamp) in `to_dict` and parse it back in `from_dict`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

false_positives.candidate:
New `assignment_source` param on `sync_status_outbound` is never passed

The abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature now takes `assignment_source`, but no caller in this PR passes it. Status-sync loops are therefore not addressed, despite the API suggesting otherwise.

The parameter is also named for assignment, which is confusing on a status-sync method. Either wire it through for status changes or drop it to avoid a misleading interface.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
MetricAlertDetectorHandler is abstract and cannot be instantiated

`MetricAlertDetectorHandler` now subclasses `StatefulDetectorHandler` but its body is just `pass`. It implements none of the abstract members: `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data`.

`MetricAlertFire.detector_handler` points at this class. `Detector.detector_handler` calls `group_type.detector_handler(self)`, so any `metric_alert_fire` detector will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class` when accessed. Inside `process_detectors` that exception propagates and aborts processing for every detector in the batch.

Previously the handler implemented `evaluate` and safely returned an empty result. Either keep a concrete stub implementing the abstract methods, or keep the old `DetectorHandler` subclass until the real implementation exists.

true_positives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Docstring still says evaluate returns a list

The `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` docstring still says it "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`". After this change it returns a dict keyed by `DetectorGroupKey`, so the docstring misleads implementers and callers about the return type.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Monitor context ignores the humanized config copy

`get_monitor_environment_context` builds `config`, a copy of the monitor config with `schedule_type` replaced by its display value. It then returns `monitor_environment.monitor.config` (the raw original) instead of that copy.

The local `config` is dead code, so the event's monitor context shows the raw integer `schedule_type` rather than the human-readable label. This bug existed before and was carried over unchanged by the move. Return `config` instead.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

false_positives.candidate:
Moved and renamed functions no longer importable from mark_failed

This PR removes several names from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed`:
- `mark_failed_threshold`, now `try_incident_threshold` in `incidents.py`
- `create_issue_platform_occurrence`, now `create_incident_occurrence` in `incident_occurrence.py`
- `get_failure_reason`
- `get_monitor_environment_context`
- `SimpleCheckIn`

No other files are updated and no compatibility re-exports are left behind. Any existing caller, test import, or `mock.patch` target that references these names in `mark_failed` will now fail with `ImportError`/`AttributeError`. Examples are tests that import `get_failure_reason` or patch `mark_failed.create_issue_platform_occurrence`.

Either update all references in the same PR or re-export the old names from `mark_failed`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent metric tag key (`shards` vs `shard`)

`spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` uses the tag key `shards`, while `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `segment_size_bytes` use `shard`. This makes it awkward to correlate these metrics in dashboards. Use one key consistently.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

The test sets `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None` at the start, so the added `time.sleep(0.1)`, meant to "give flusher threads time to process", does nothing. The test still depends on `join()` busy-waiting. The comment is misleading, and the test may be flaky if it relies on this delay.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unhealthy spawn processes are never killed before a replacement starts

Processes are created with `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which builds a `SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` subclasses `BaseProcess`, not `multiprocessing.Process`, so `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is always False and `kill()` is never called.

The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. Now, when a flusher is detected as hung, the old process keeps running while a new one is spawned for the same shards. Two flushers then work the same Redis shards concurrently, which can produce duplicate or fragmented segments. Leaked processes also pile up on every restart.

Fix: check against `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` (or `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`).

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

The test sets `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None` at the start, so the added `time.sleep(0.1)`, meant to "give flusher threads time to process", does nothing. The test still depends on `join()` busy-waiting. The comment is misleading, and the test may be flaky if it relies on this delay.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() skips cleanup of remaining processes once the deadline passes

`next_step.join(timeout)` can use up the whole timeout. After that, the per-process loop hits `break` on `remaining_time <= 0` and leaves the loop without terminating any remaining processes. With N flusher processes, any not yet visited stay alive and are never terminated.

The deadline should only cap the wait. Termination of every process should still happen after the loop.

false_positives.candidate:
Dead code: `_create_process_for_shard` is never used

`_create_process_for_shard` is not called anywhere. Restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards` directly, so this method should be removed.

Memory info is queried once per flusher buffer

`get_memory_info()` is called on every per-process `SpansBuffer`. If these buffers share the same Redis cluster, every node's memory is queried and summed N times on each `submit`.

The ratio stays correct, but this adds N-fold Redis INFO calls on the consumer's main thread, which this PR is trying to keep minimal. Querying once (e.g. via the original buffer) would be sufficient.

Unrelated documentation change bundled in PR

The hasattr/isinstance anti-pattern added to CLAUDE.md has nothing to do with the multiprocessed span flusher. It should go in a separate PR.

join() never terminates spawn processes

The `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` check in `join()` has the same flaw: `SpawnProcess` is not a subclass of `multiprocessing.Process`. As a result, `terminate()` is never called on flusher processes that are still alive after the wait loop. Lingering flushers can keep flushing shards that have been reassigned to another consumer after a rebalance or shutdown.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error-handling test asserts no commit, contradicting both docstring and implementation

`test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` says errors shouldn't block commits for other messages. However, it asserts `test_partition not in committed_offsets`.

The worker marks offsets complete even when processing raises, so the 1s commit loop will commit offset 102. The test only passes if it finishes before the commit thread wakes up, which makes it timing-dependent and flaky. It also asserts the wrong behavior.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs on its own daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function(...)`, which wraps arroyo's `Commit` callback. That callback is meant to be called from the strategy's `submit`/`poll` on the StreamProcessor thread. It mutates the processor's staged offsets and consumer state without any locking.

Calling it concurrently with the main loop is a data race on the consumer/commit state. It can also fire after the partition was revoked, staging offsets for partitions the consumer no longer owns.

Committable offsets should be computed here, but the actual commit should happen in `poll()` on the main thread.

Commits stall forever on non-contiguous Kafka offsets

`get_committable_offsets` walks every integer from `last_committed+1` and stops at the first offset not in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed contiguous: transactional control markers and log compaction leave gaps.

When that happens, the missing offset is never added, so the loop breaks there on every pass. Commits for that partition stop permanently and memory grows.

The logic should compute the highest offset below the minimum outstanding offset among those actually seen, rather than requiring every integer to be present.

Shared queue pool is shut down on rebalance, so later messages are skipped and committed

`ResultsStrategyFactory` creates one `FixedQueuePool` in `__init__` and passes it to every strategy built by `create_with_partitions`. On a partition revoke, arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the old strategy, and `close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`. That stops all workers and shuts down every queue.

On reassignment, `create_with_partitions` hands the same dead pool to the new strategy (the `assert self.queue_pool is not None` passes). Each `work_queue.put()` then raises `queue.ShutDown`. The broad `except` in `submit()` catches it, logs it, and marks the offset complete.

Result: after the first rebalance, every message is silently dropped and its offset committed, so uptime results are permanently lost. The pool's lifetime should belong to the factory, or each strategy should get its own pool. The tracker state for revoked partitions (`last_committed`, outstanding offsets) should also be cleared.

Unbounded queues, no backpressure

Each `queue.Queue()` is created without `maxsize`, and `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`. The class docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing implements it.

If one group's queue is slow (the exact scenario this PR targets), the consumer keeps pulling messages from Kafka and buffering them in memory without limit. That can lead to OOM, and the outstanding offset sets grow without bound as well.

Use bounded queues and raise `MessageRejected` when a queue, or the total backlog, is full.

close() stops committing before draining, and drops queued work

`close()` sets `shutdown_event` and joins the commit thread first, then shuts down the pool. Offsets completed during the drain are therefore never committed.

The pool's `shutdown()` also sets `worker.shutdown = True` before shutting down the queues. Each worker exits its loop after the current item, so the remaining queued items are abandoned rather than drained.

`join(timeout)` ignores its timeout, and the internal joins can block for up to 5s × (1 + num_queues), which may exceed arroyo's join timeout and hold up rebalances. The pool should drain, then do a final commit, then stop.

queue.ShutDown / Queue.shutdown require Python 3.13

`queue.ShutDown` and `Queue.shutdown()` were added in Python 3.13. On any older runtime, the `except queue.ShutDown` clause raises `AttributeError` when evaluated, and `shutdown()` fails (that error is swallowed by the broad except). Confirm the deployed interpreter version, or use a sentinel-based shutdown instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test does not prove the deny entry short-circuits the check

The comment says the permCache entry allows access "to prove this is not checked". But the entry is `{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`, and `checkPermission` treats a false value as no grant.

The Check would also fall through to the DB via the default `fakeStore`, which has no permissions. The request would be denied even without the denial cache, so the test passes regardless of whether the denial cache works. Set the value to `true` so the test actually checks precedence.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Ambiguous `_` separator lets denial keys for different resources collide

The denial key joins name and parent folder with `_`, and Grafana UIDs commonly contain underscores. For example, (name="a_b", parent="c") and (name="a", parent="b_c") both produce `...action_a_b_c`. Action and user UID are joined the same way.

A denial cached for one resource can therefore wrongly deny access to a different resource for the TTL. Use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs, or encode or length-prefix each component.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

false_positives.candidate:
Caching a denial reintroduces the stale-access problem for newly created resources

A denial is now cached for 30s right after a fresh DB lookup returns not-allowed. On later calls the denial-cache check at the top of Check returns early, so the DB is not re-queried.

If any Check for a resource runs before its creator's permission rows are committed, the creator is locked out of the new resource for the full TTL. Examples are the apiserver reading back the object during or right after create, or a UI poll. Likewise, permissions granted to a user right after a denial are ignored for 30s.

This is exactly the scenario the PR is meant to fix. Consider a much shorter TTL for denials, invalidating denial entries when permissions or resources change, or not caching denials for named resources.

Denial cache key omits identity type, so anonymous and renderer share deny entries

`userPermDenialCacheKey` is built from the raw `checkReq.UserUID` and never includes the identity type. Both `anonymous:0` and `render:0` parse to UID "0", so they get the same denial key.

The renderer is supposed to be able to read every dashboard and folder. Suppose an anonymous Check is denied for some dashboard. That denial is cached, and for the next 30s a renderer Check for the same action and dashboard returns the cached deny without ever reaching `getRendererPermissions`. Dashboard rendering then fails intermittently.

The same risk applies to any identity types whose raw UIDs overlap. Include the identity type, or the resolved identifier, in the key.

Remote/cloud client keeps a 30s client-side cache, so the creator issue persists there

Only the in-proc client switches to `NoopCache`. In cloud mode, `newRemoteRBACClient` still caches Check results client-side for 30s.

The server-side re-query on a missing scope never runs for a decision the client already cached. A creator in cloud mode can still be denied access to a dashboard or folder they just created.

User identifier lookup is repeated on failure

`getCachedIdentityPermissions` calls `GetUserIdentifiers`, which falls through to the DB on a cache miss. If that call errors, the error is swallowed and `getIdentityPermissions` immediately calls `GetUserIdentifiers` again, issuing a second identical DB query.

The same happens in List. It is wasted load in the error path, for example when a user is not found.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing `key` prop on GrafanaRuleListItem in mapped list

As new pages are appended via infinite scroll, item state (open dropdowns, delete modals, silence drawers) can end up attached to the wrong rule. Pass `key={key}`.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence menu item is a no-op when only promRule is provided

`AlertRuleMenu` now shows 'Silence notifications' based on the prom-rule ability. Clicking it sets `showSilenceDrawer=true`, but the drawer only renders when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true. In the list view `rule` (the ruler rule) is undefined, so nothing opens. Users see an action that silently does nothing.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete and Pause menu items can never appear in the list view

The list view now passes only `promRule`, so `rulerRule` is undefined. The Delete item requires `canDelete && rulerRule`, and Pause (line 123) requires `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`.
