Export and Pause no longer supported for Grafana recording rules

The ruler-based abilities gated ModifyExport, Pause and Restore on `isGrafanaManagedAlertRule`, which is true for any Grafana rule including recording rules. The prom-based version uses `isAlertingRule` (`prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule`), which is false for recording rules. As a result, Grafana-managed recording rules can no longer be exported, paused, restored or permanently deleted from the list view, even though this is supported. Use `prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)` here instead.

Federated rule check removed from legacy useAllAlertRuleAbilities

`useAllAlertRuleAbilities` previously computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`. It now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, which hardcodes `isFederated = false`. Federated Mimir rule groups shown through CombinedRule-based components (the existing list, RulesTable, rule viewer) are no longer treated as immutable. Update and Delete become available for rules that should not be edited there. Pass the federation info through or keep the check in the CombinedRule wrapper.

returnTo parameter dropped from rule view link

The previous implementation built the view href with `createRelativeUrl(..., { returnTo })`, using `createReturnTo()`. The new item omits `returnTo`. Navigating back from the rule detail page no longer restores the user's list filters and position.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
$__range detection now runs on already-interpolated expressions

`querySupportsSplitting` uses `isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` to keep queries containing `$__range` out of time splitting. Because interpolation now happens on line 299, before the partition, `$__range` (and `$__auto` resolved to a range) has already been replaced by a concrete duration. The check therefore no longer matches, and these queries are silently split into per-day chunks. That is exactly the case the guard and its comment were written to prevent. The range-variable check should run on the raw expression before interpolation.

Interpolated targets are re-interpolated inside runSplitQuery

`runShardSplitQuery` interpolates the targets, injects shard selectors, and then passes each sub-request to `runSplitQuery`. `runSplitQuery` calls `applyTemplateVariables` again on those already-interpolated, shard-modified expressions, using the same `scopedVars` and `filters`. This double pass is redundant and risks re-applying ad-hoc filters. It also lets the second pass alter the injected `__stream_shard__` matchers or user values that contain `$`. Interpolation should be done in only one of the two places, for example via a flag or by keeping it in the shared entry point.

Queries are now template-interpolated more than once

`runSplitQuery` now calls `datasource.applyTemplateVariables` on every target, but the same request still goes through `datasource.runQuery`, which normally applies template variables again before sending to the backend. On the sharding path it is worse: `runShardSplitQuery` interpolates first, then `runSplitQuery` interpolates every sub-request again. The updated test confirms this, expecting 5 calls for 4 requests.

Loki's `applyTemplateVariables` is not idempotent. It appends ad-hoc filters (`request.filters`), so each pass can add those matchers again. It also re-runs variable replacement on already-interpolated text, so a variable value that contains `$something` or regex-escaped characters is substituted or escaped a second time. The result is duplicated filters, wrong expressions, and wasted work.

Interpolation should happen exactly once: either skip it in `runSplitQuery` when called from the shard path, or remove it from the downstream `runQuery` path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
ContextualLoggerMiddleware dereferences req without a nil check

`QueryData`, `CallResource`, `CheckHealth` and `CollectMetrics` read `req.PluginContext` unconditionally. A nil request therefore panics here. `LoggerMiddleware`, the next middleware, explicitly guards against `req == nil` and passes the call through. The two adjacent middlewares are inconsistent, and the new one panics where the old logging path tolerated nil. Add the same nil guard, or document that requests are never nil.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, so logged calls are lost

`TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()` instead of `f`. `LoggerMiddleware` now logs only through `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`, so every log call goes to a throwaway instance. The `InfoLogs`/`ErrorLogs` counters on the TestLogger handed to the middleware never change. Any test asserting on what the middleware logged will silently see zero calls. `New` has the same problem. Return `f` so calls are recorded on the logger the test holds.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.

false_positives.candidate:
Adding FromContext to the Logger interface breaks other implementations

Adding a method to the exported `plog.Logger` interface is a breaking change. Any other implementation inside or outside this package (fakes, wrappers, enterprise code) will no longer compile until it implements `FromContext`. The doc comment is also inaccurate: it says the returned logger has "this logger's context plus the given context", but it actually adds the contextual attributes stored in the `context.Context`.

Request log fields now depend implicitly on ContextualLoggerMiddleware ordering

`pluginId`, `endpoint`, `uname`, `dsName`, `dsUID` and `traceID` used to be added explicitly in `logRequest`. They are now expected to come from the context via `FromContext`. That only works if `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` runs earlier in the chain and the infra logger's context provider supplies `traceID`. If `LoggerMiddleware` is used on its own, or the middlewares are reordered, the 'Plugin Request Completed' log line silently loses these identifying fields. Dashboards and alerts built on the grafana-data-egress event depend on them. Document the ordering requirement or keep the essential fields explicit.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Count-then-insert is not atomic, so concurrent devices can exceed the limit

`CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices` and then the upsert as separate statements, with no transaction or lock. Several new devices arriving at the same time can all read `count < deviceLimit` and all insert. The configured limit can then be exceeded under load, and there is no later reconciliation.

true_positives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device tagging moved onto the synchronous auth path

`TagDevice` used to run in a background goroutine with its own timeout. It now runs inline in `Authenticate` using the request context. On a cache miss it does a COUNT query plus an upsert or update on the request path, which adds DB latency to anonymous requests. A slow DB, or a request context that is cancelled, now directly delays or affects authentication. The panic recovery from the goroutine version was also removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
RowsAffected==0 is treated as limit reached, which misfires on MySQL no-op updates

Once the limit is reached, `updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` whenever `RowsAffected()` is 0. By default MySQL reports only rows whose values actually changed. `updated_at` has second precision, so a repeat update for an existing device in the same second with the same IP and user agent reports 0 rows. That registered, legitimate device is then rejected as over the limit. The update should check that the device exists rather than relying on rows changed (or use CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS).

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Local cache entry set before the limit check lets rejected devices in on retry

`tagDeviceUI` calls `localCache.SetDefault(key, ...)` before `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. If the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the first request is rejected, but the cache key stays set. For the next ~29 minutes, `TagDevice` for that device returns nil from the cache hit, and `Authenticate` lets the request through. The device limit is effectively enforced only on a device's first request per cache window. The cache entry should be set only after a successful write, or removed when the write fails.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
30-day expiration constant duplicated in several places

`anonymousDeviceExpiration` is defined separately in `anonstore/database.go` and `api/api.go`, and `thirtyDays` remains in `impl.go`. These define the same counting window. If they drift apart, the device list, the usage stats and the limit enforcement would use different windows. Export a single constant from `anonstore` and use it everywhere.

ProvideAnonDBStore signature change may break the wire provider set

`ProvideAnonDBStore` now takes a `deviceLimit int64`, and `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` builds the store itself. If the wire provider sets (wire.go / wireexts) still register `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` and bind `AnonStore`, injector generation will fail. Either no int64 provider exists, or the provider is now unused. Those wire files are not updated in this PR.

Raw store error returned to the auth broker when the limit is reached

`Authenticate` returns the plain `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached` error, not an authn-specific error. The user probably gets a generic authentication failure with no clear message that the anonymous device limit was hit, and operators may struggle to diagnose why anonymous users are being rejected.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Debug logging left at Error level, dumping full ID lists

The cleanup loops call r.log.Error on every batch, with messages like "Annotations to clean by time", "cleaned annotations by time", "Tags to clean" and "cleaned tags". These calls fire even when nothing failed, so normal operation floods the logs with error-level entries. The "ids" field includes the whole ID slice, which can hold up to the batch size (tens of thousands of IDs). This looks like leftover debugging. Remove these calls, or lower them to Debug and drop the full ID list.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute

The cleanup service interval changes from 10 minutes to 1 minute, but each run still has a 9-minute timeout. All cleanup jobs (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, etc.) would now run 10x more often, adding database load and overlapping work. Nothing in the PR description justifies this, so it looks like a leftover from local testing.

false_positives.candidate:
Quadratic string building for inlined IDs

The inlined ID list is built with repeated fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v), which copies the growing string on every iteration. With batch sizes around 32767 this is O(n^2) allocation and copying on each batch. Use strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt into a byte slice instead.

SQLite inlining decision based on configured batch size, not actual parameter count

The choice to inline IDs instead of binding parameters checks r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize, not len(ids). This matches today's code paths, but it is fragile coupling. If deleteByIDs is ever called with more IDs than the configured batch size, it will exceed SQLite's 999-variable limit and fail. Basing the check on len(ids) would be correct regardless of configuration.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete attaches the base logger to the context instead of the enriched one

`ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` drops the name, kind and method values built into `log` on the previous line. Downstream logging in Delete therefore lacks that context, unlike the other methods, which pass `log`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete success metric uses object name as kind label

`d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object name where the kind is expected. This puts the wrong value in the kind label and creates an unbounded set of metric label values (cardinality explosion). It should pass `options.Kind`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and get cancelled when the request returns

The goroutines for Create (line 51), Update (135), Delete (110) and DeleteCollection (163) build their timeout context from the incoming request `ctx`. The apiserver cancels that context as soon as the handler returns, which is right after the goroutine is launched. The legacy write will therefore often fail with `context canceled`, or never really run, so the 'safety' write to legacy is unreliable. Derive the context with `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` before adding the timeout.

Duplicate go.work.sum entry and unrelated dependency churn

This diff adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod`, which already appears a few lines above. It also adds several unrelated otel/alertmanager sums. This looks like accidental tooling churn that doesn't belong in this PR.

Input object shared with background goroutine (data race)

The goroutine passes `obj` to `Legacy.Create` while the handler goes on to serialize and return `created`. Storage implementations may mutate `obj` in place or return the same pointer, so legacy conversion and response encoding can touch the same object concurrently. Pass a deep copy (`obj.DeepCopyObject()`) to the async write.

Legacy DeleteCollection recorded as storage duration

The async legacy DeleteCollection goroutine calls `recordStorageDuration` instead of `recordLegacyDuration`. Legacy latencies and errors are therefore counted under the storage metric, which skews both series.

Legacy update re-applies objInfo against legacy state instead of using the storage result

The old code wrapped the object returned by storage in `updateWrapper` before calling legacy. The new code passes the raw `objInfo` to `Legacy.Update`, so `UpdatedObject` is evaluated against whatever legacy currently holds. That legacy state may be stale or missing, especially for patches, and the stores can diverge. Running this concurrently after the request also lets the patch/transform functions be reused outside the request lifetime.

Legacy write errors in the goroutines are silently dropped

In every async goroutine the legacy error is only turned into a boolean metric label and is never logged. When a legacy write fails, nothing records which object, name or kind failed, so it is impossible to diagnose or reconcile the divergence between the two stores. Log the error together with the object identity.

Mode 3 integration tests may be flaky due to async legacy writes

`doPlaylistTests` compares the legacy API with the k8s API immediately after k8s writes (create, then legacy list; update, then `getFromBothAPIs`). In mode 3 the legacy write happens asynchronously, so if the legacy endpoints read from legacy storage these assertions race with the background write.

Storage failure recorded as legacy duration in Create and Update

When `d.Storage.Create` fails (line 45), and likewise `d.Storage.Update` (line 129), the code calls `recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` even though the call that failed was to unified storage. The result is wrong metrics: phantom legacy errors and missing storage errors. Use `recordStorageDuration` here.

Unit tests don't verify or synchronize the async legacy writes

Legacy and storage share one mock, and the tests never wait for or assert the legacy goroutine calls. Nothing checks that legacy is actually written, and goroutines may still call into the mock after the subtest finishes, which can cause flaky failures. Some cases also configure legacy expectations that never matter, such as the Create error case.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not re-checked after taking the write lock, so concurrent callers all reload the manifest

`GetWebAssets` reads the cache under `RLock`, releases it, then takes the write `Lock` and unconditionally rebuilds `entryPointAssetsCache`. In non-Dev mode, N requests can arrive while the cache is still empty (for example at startup). All of them see `ret == nil`, queue on `Lock()`, and each in turn reopens and re-parses `assets-manifest.json`, overwriting the cache with a fresh pointer. If the CDN path were enabled, each would also make its own HTTP request while holding the exclusive lock. This adds avoidable I/O and latency, and different callers get different `*EntryPointAssets` instances. Fix: right after `Lock()`, check again `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` (double-checked locking), or use `sync.Once` / `singleflight` for the non-dev path.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false through misleading logic

`enableSqlExpressions` reads the `sqlExpressions` feature flag, negates it into a variable named `enabled`, and then returns `false` on both branches. The flag lookup has no effect, and the name and structure suggest the toggle still controls the feature when it does not. A future maintainer could "fix" the inverted-looking logic and silently re-enable the vulnerable path. Replace it with an explicit, commented hard-disable (e.g. `return false // disabled due to CVE-2024-9264`), or remove the helper and return the error directly in the `QueryTypeSQL` case.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Existing parser/SQL command tests will now fail

`TablesList` now uses the stub `NewInMemoryDB()`, whose `RunCommands` always returns "not implemented". `NewSQLCommand` and `Execute` likewise always fail. Any existing tests that assert table extraction or SQL execution results (e.g. `pkg/expr/sql/parser_test.go`, `pkg/expr/sql_command_test.go`, SQL cases in the expr reader/service tests) will now fail. None of them are updated or skipped in this PR, so the change will likely break CI, or leave tests that silently assert on behaviour that no longer exists.

false_positives.candidate:
Injection-prone SQL construction left in place behind a stub

`TablesList` still builds `SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')` by string formatting user input, with only single-quote doubling as protection. This pattern is the attack surface behind the CVE. It is now inert only because the stub DB always errors. Anyone who later swaps a real engine back into `NewInMemoryDB` would immediately reintroduce the vulnerable code path. Remove the dead SQL-building code, or clearly mark it as unsafe.

Legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand path bypasses the new gate and fails with an opaque error

The new disable check lives only in `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery`. `UnmarshalSQLCommand`, used by the rawNode/legacy pipeline, still calls `NewSQLCommand`. That call now fails inside the `TablesList` stub, so users get a generic "error reading SQL command" BadRequest instead of a clear "SQL expressions are disabled" message. The protection is not applied in one central place, so a future change to the stub could re-open this path. Put the disable check in `NewSQLCommand` or `UnmarshalSQLCommand` as well.

Misleading error returned even when the feature flag is enabled

The `QueryTypeSQL` case returns "sqlExpressions is not implemented" for every request, including from users who explicitly turned on the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle. That wording reads like a missing build or feature rather than a deliberate security disable, which will cause confusion and support load. Use a clearer message, e.g. "SQL expressions are disabled", and consider logging or deprecating the flag.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Finer-grained lock allows duplicate concurrent builds of the same index

The lock that serialized all of `BuildIndex` is gone, and nothing deduplicates builds per key. `getOrCreateIndex` is a check-then-act sequence (`GetIndex`, then `build`), so concurrent Search requests or watch events for the same NamespacedResource can each build a full index.

Consequences:
- The last writer wins in the cache, and the other built indexes are simply discarded, wasting work.
- `IndexTenants` and `IndexedKinds` metrics are incremented more than once.
- For file-based indexes, the second `bleve.New(dir)` on the same directory fails (path exists) and the request errors.

Fix: use a per-key lock or singleflight around the build.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the index cache without a lock while builds can write to it

`TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` without taking `cacheMu`. This PR adds a call to `s.search.TotalDocs()` in `searchSupport.init` (search.go:216). That call runs after the watch goroutine has already started (search.go:207).

The watch goroutine calls `handleEvent` → `getOrCreateIndex` → `BuildIndex`, which writes `b.cache[key]` under `cacheMu.Lock()`. Because `TotalDocs` holds no lock, a map write during its iteration is possible. That is a data race, and Go may abort the process with "concurrent map iteration and map write" during startup.

Fix: take `b.cacheMu.RLock()` in `TotalDocs`.

false_positives.candidate:
After Stop, RPC handlers keep serving because the Init checks were removed

`Stop` still sets `s.initErr` to "service is stopping" / "service is stopped". Previously every handler called `s.Init(ctx)`, which returned `initErr`, so requests were rejected after shutdown.

This PR removed those calls from every handler. `initErr` is now effectively dead after construction, and Read/List/Create/Watch keep executing against a cancelled backend and broadcaster after Stop.

Fix: either add an explicit stopped check to the handlers or remove this misleading state.

Constructor now blocks on DB init and full index build; context leaked on failure

`NewResourceServer` now synchronously runs `lifecycle.Init` (DB connect/ping) and builds every search index. That makes construction slow, and it fails hard if the DB is unreachable at construction time; any caller relying on lazy init (e.g. wire/DI graphs, tests building a server without a ready DB) will break.

Also, on the error path the function returns `nil, err` without calling `cancel()`, so the cancelable context is leaked. Any goroutines started by a partial init keep running.

Integration test disabled for postgres

The storage-server integration test is now skipped on postgres, with only a TODO and no linked issue. Since this PR changes startup behaviour (init in the constructor), this loses coverage exactly where regressions are likely. It may also be hiding a real startup failure introduced by this change.

Shared variables mutated from errgroup goroutines

Inside `group.Go`, each worker writes the outer `err` (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and increments `totalBatchesIndexed` without synchronization. With `initWorkers > 1` these are data races.

The span attribute `namespaced_indexed` can be wrong. The returned error may also belong to a different goroutine than the one that failed.

This matters more now that the PR targets high-concurrency builds. Fix: use local variables inside the goroutine and an atomic counter.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup registers removal of a literal "alias" IDP instead of the created ones

The new test registers its cleanup as `testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove`. That targets an IDP whose alias is literally "alias", not the `idp-alias-N` providers just created. The same mistake appears at line 425 for `idp-alias-20`.

The cleanup therefore never removes the 21 IDPs this test creates. They stay in the test realm and can skew later tests that count login IDPs or rely on cache state. Use the actual alias variable when registering the cleanup.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Global login predicate semantics changed to exclude non-public org IDPs

`LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate()` is a public SPI helper. It now also requires org-linked IDPs to have `BROKER_PUBLIC=true`.

This was added to support cache-invalidation decisions, but it silently changes behaviour for every other caller of the predicate. For example, flows that legitimately show an organization's non-public brokers after the user has identified the org would now filter those brokers out.

It also means the predicate disagrees with the `getForLogin` javadoc, which describes eligibility without mentioning publicity. Consider keeping the SPI predicate unchanged and applying the broker-public check locally in the cache invalidation logic.

Update invalidation compares org-aware wrapped model against raw model

In `update()`, `idpById` comes from `getById`, which returns the org-aware wrapper. That wrapper's `isEnabled()` also depends on whether the organization (and the org feature) is enabled. The incoming `model` is a plain `IdentityProviderModel`.

When the linked org is disabled, the login predicate gives different results for `original` and `updated` even if the IDP's own fields are unchanged. The login caches are then invalidated needlessly.

For correct comparisons, base the decision on the IDP's stored fields (for example `idpDelegate.getById`) rather than the wrapper.

remove() now always performs an extra DB lookup

`remove()` now unconditionally calls `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)`, bypassing the cache. Previously this lookup was only done on the `isInvalid` path, where the cached copy was unusable.

Every IDP removal now issues an additional database query even when a valid cached entry exists. The cached entry could be used to evaluate the login predicate instead.

If `storedIdp` is null on the invalid path, `registerIDPInvalidation(storedIdp)` throws an NPE. That behaviour is pre-existing, but this refactor makes it easier to hit.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default KeyStore provider and builds a KeyStore on every call

`getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, typically `SUN`. This is not a BouncyCastle provider.

Code that relies on `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER` (derived from this method) will request algorithms from that provider by name. For example `KeyFactory.getInstance(alg, "SUN")` will fail with NoSuchAlgorithmException for most algorithms.

It also instantiates a new KeyStore on every call. Return a cached provider, and document clearly that this is not BC.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code: encoders created and discarded

Lines 114-115 call `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger)` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger)` and throw away the results. The same encoders are built again inside `writeDerSeq` just below. This is leftover code that should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Indefinite-length (-1) handling yields incorrect reads

`readLength` returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding, and callers do not handle it.
- In `readSequence`, the loop exits immediately.
- In `readNext`, `length += reset()` produces a wrong small length, so `read(length)` returns a truncated element.
- In `readInteger`, `new byte[-1]` throws `NegativeArraySizeException`, an unchecked exception instead of `IOException`.

DER never allows indefinite length, so reject it explicitly with an `IOException`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract interface method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

`int order()` is added as an abstract method on the public `CryptoProvider` SPI. Any external or custom implementation (custom crypto providers, the separate keycloak-client repository) will no longer compile. Already-compiled ones will throw `AbstractMethodError` when `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` calls `order()` during sorting.

Suggested fix: declare it as a `default` method returning a neutral value (e.g. 0 or 200) to keep the SPI backward compatible.

false_positives.candidate:
Removing the multiple-provider error lets equal-order providers be picked silently (FIPS vs non-FIPS)

Before this change, `detectProvider` threw when more than one CryptoProvider was found. Now it sorts by `order()` and takes the first. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return 200.

If two of them end up on the classpath (for example a misconfigured FIPS distribution that also ships the default crypto jar), the stable sort falls back to ServiceLoader/classpath order. One provider is chosen arbitrarily, and the conflict is reported only at debug level. A FIPS deployment could silently run with the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider.

Suggested fix: keep failing (or at least warn loudly) when the top two providers share the same order. Only the lower-priority fallback (the authz-client provider at 100) should be ignored silently.

Test uses a single default-size EC key for ES384/ES512, so P-384/P-521 paths are never exercised

The key pair is generated with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` using the default curve, typically P-256. That same key is used for ES256, ES384 and ES512, so r and s are always about 32 bytes.

Untested paths:
- 48- and 66-byte integers.
- The ES512 case, where the DER sequence exceeds 127 bytes and the long-form length code in `ASN1Encoder.writeLength` and `ASN1Decoder.readLength` is needed.

The test also only round-trips through the custom code. It never checks the DER output with `Signature.verify` or against the BC implementation, so a symmetric bug would pass.

Suggested fix: initialize the generator with the matching curve for each algorithm (secp256r1, secp384r1, secp521r1) and verify the re-encoded DER signature with the JDK.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removal listener now gated on V1 only: V2 resources are orphaned and V1+V2 together throws

The role/client/group removal listener now runs only when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) is enabled. This has two consequences.

1. With only V2 enabled, deleting a client never cleans up its admin-permission resource. That resource is named after the client id and lives in the admin-permissions client. Any scope permissions referencing it are left dangling, so stale grants and resources accumulate.

2. When V1 and V2 are both enabled, `management()` returns `MgmtPermissionsV2`. `ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`, so the `ClientRemovedEvent` handler fails and client deletion breaks.

The listener should check which version is active. For V2 it should remove or detach the V2 resources/permissions instead of calling the V1-only API.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Possible NPE when the all-clients resource is missing

When no per-client resource exists, `hasPermission` falls back to `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...)`. That method can return null, for example when the schema is not supported for the server or the 'Clients' resource is absent in a realm initialized before this type was added.

The null is passed straight to `findByResource(server, resource)` and later dereferenced via `resource.getScopes()`. The result is an NPE instead of a clean `false`. A null check is needed, matching what the sibling `hasPermission(String)` does.

true_positives.golden_comment: Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code and unused imports

Several pieces of `ClientPermissionsV2` are never used:
- the private method `getEvaluationContext`
- the `logger` field
- the imports `Scope` and the static `TOKEN_EXCHANGE`

They appear to be copied from V1 and should be removed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

false_positives.candidate:
Existing realms never get the new Clients resource/scopes

`init()` returns early if the admin-permissions client already exists. Scopes and type resources are created only on first initialization.

Realms that were initialized before this change therefore lack the new scopes (`configure`, `map-roles-client-scope`, `map-roles-composite`) and the 'Clients' all-resource. In those realms, `getOrCreateResource` for a client throws `ModelException("No scopes found.")`. Creating all-clients permissions also cannot work.

A migration or idempotent sync of schema scopes and resources is needed.

getResourceName not extended for Clients type

`getResourceName` maps user resources to usernames and the type resource to "All users". There is no equivalent branch for the new Clients type.

As a result, client permissions display the raw internal client UUID, or 'Clients' for the all-resource, instead of the clientId or "All clients". This makes permission listings confusing.

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Exit code 4 changes meaning from 'recreate required' to 'feature disabled'

Previously the `check` command exited with 4 when a recreate upgrade was required. Now 3 means recreate and 4 means the `rolling-updates` feature is disabled. Any automation written against the earlier release that maps 4 to 'recreate' and everything else to 'error' will now treat a recreate result (3) as an unexpected failure. This matches the docs, which already listed 3, but the change is incompatible with earlier releases and should be called out in release/upgrade notes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

false_positives.candidate:
Documented command overrides the user's own `features` configuration

The `updatecompatibility` macro now hard-codes `--features=rolling-updates` onto every documented `update-compatibility` command. A CLI `--features` value takes precedence over `features` set in `keycloak.conf` or `KC_FEATURES`, and it replaces them rather than adding to them. Users who already enable other features and copy the documented command will generate or check metadata against a different feature set than their real deployment. This contradicts the guide's own warning that all configuration options must be included. The docs should tell users to add `rolling-updates` to their existing feature list, not append a standalone `--features` flag.

Feature-disabled test doesn't check exit code or cover the `check` subcommand

`testFeatureNotEnabled` only checks the error message for the `metadata` subcommand. It does not assert the new documented exit code 4 (`CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED`), which is the contract scripts are told to rely on. It also never runs the `check` subcommand with the feature disabled. A regression in the exit code, or in the `check` path, would go unnoticed.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() grants manage rights to callers who only have VIEW on groups

`GroupPermissionsV2.canManage()` returns `hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)`. Because of this, an admin with only an all-groups `view` permission is treated as able to manage all groups.

`canManage()` guards `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup` (`requireManage()`). As a result, a read-only group admin can create top-level groups and move existing groups to the top level.

This is a privilege escalation. Only the `MANAGE` scope should be checked here. The interface javadoc repeats the same mistake and should be corrected too.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns authz resource IDs, not group IDs, and searches by the wrong type

The method iterates `findByType(server, "Groups")`. Per-group resources created by `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` never get a type set, so they are not found. Only the all-groups "Groups" resource has this type.

It then calls `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...)`. That method does `findByName(server, groupId)`, but resource names are group IDs, not resource IDs. The lookup therefore always falls back to the all-groups resource.

Finally, it adds `groupResource.getId()` (an authorization resource ID) to the result set, which callers treat as group IDs. The set is passed to `UserModel.GROUPS` session filtering in `UsersResource`/`BruteForceUsersResource` and to `getUsersCount(..., groupIds)`. Possible effects:
- user search is constrained to a nonexistent group ID, so no users are returned;
- counts are wrong;
- pagination breaks, because filtering otherwise happens only post-query.

The method should iterate the group resources (by name) and return `resource.getName()`.

false_positives.candidate:
Group removal listener now calls a V2 method that throws UnsupportedOperationException

`MgmtPermissionsV2.groups()` now returns `GroupPermissionsV2`, whose `setPermissionsEnabled` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`.

The listener registered here calls `management(...).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false)` on every `GroupRemovedEvent`. When V2 is enabled, `management()` returns `MgmtPermissionsV2`. Previously V2 used the V1 `GroupPermissions` here, so this path did not throw.

If both ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ and ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 are enabled, deleting a group will now fail. The listener should skip V2, or the V2 implementation should be a no-op.

Public utility method removed without deprecation

The public static method `ModelToRepresentation.searchGroupModelsByAttributes` is removed outright. `ModelToRepresentation` is a utility class that custom extensions can call, so any extension using this method will break at compile or link time.

Consider deprecating the method first and removing it later.

Wrong javadoc for requireManageMembers

The javadoc for `requireManageMembers` says it throws if `canManageMembership(GroupModel)` returns false. It actually delegates to `canManageMembers(GroupModel)`, so the reference is wrong and misleading.

true_positives.golden_comment: The translation is in Italian instead of Lithuanian. This should be translated to Lithuanian to match the file's locale (messages_lt.properties).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Lithuanian translation replaced with Italian text

`totpStep1` in the Lithuanian bundle was replaced with `Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:`, which is Italian, apparently copied from messages_it. Lithuanian users will see an Italian sentence. The same mistake appears for `loginTotpStep1` in themes/.../login/messages/messages_lt.properties. Both need a proper Lithuanian translation, or the key should be removed so it falls back to English.

true_positives.golden_comment: The totpStep1 value uses Traditional Chinese terms in the Simplified Chinese file (zh_CN), which is likely incorrect for this locale. Please verify the locale‑appropriate translation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Traditional Chinese text in the Simplified Chinese bundle

The new `totpStep1` value `在您的手機上安裝以下應用程式之一：` uses Traditional characters and Taiwanese wording (手機, 應用程式) in the zh_CN bundle. The rest of the file is Simplified Chinese. It should be something like `在您的手机上安装以下应用之一：`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.
The method name 'santizeAnchors' should be 'sanitizeAnchors' (missing 'i').
Field HTML_TAGS should be declared as 'private static final' following Java naming conventions for constants

false_positives.candidate:
ANCHOR_PATTERN also matches tags that start with 'a'

`</?a[^>]*>` matches `<abbr>`, `<address>`, `<area>`, `<audio>` and similar tags, not just `<a ...>`. Such tags are then treated as anchors and must match the English source exactly, which gives confusing 'anchor tag' errors. The pattern should require a word boundary after `a`, e.g. `</?a(\s[^>]*)?>`.

Anchor mismatch message omits key and file

`Didn't find anchor tag ... in original string` does not include the key or the file name. Every other message from this verifier does. When the build fails on this check across dozens of property files, the offending entry is hard to find.

Diff-trimming logic can throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException

The prefix length `start` and suffix length `end` are computed independently, so they can overlap. Example: value="aa", sanitized="a" gives start=1 and end=1. Then `sanitized.substring(1, 0)` throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. Instead of reporting an 'Illegal HTML' message, the verifier crashes the build for exactly the inputs it is meant to report, such as a removed duplicated character or tag. The suffix scan should be bounded so that `end <= min(value.length(), sanitized.length()) - start`.

Java MessageFormat syntax introduced into an i18next bundle

This bundle is used by the React account console through i18next. Every other entry here uses `{{0}}` interpolation. The new value uses Java MessageFormat placeholders (`{0}`, `{1}`, `{2}`) plus a `{2,choice,...}` pattern, and i18next does not interpret either. Users will see the literal text `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.` instead of the attribute name, the numbers and the pluralised word. The previous `{{0}}`-based value should be kept, or pluralisation should be done with i18next.

Java choice format used in admin-ui i18next messages

This is the admin console (React/i18next) bundle, which interpolates `{{n}}`. The `error-invalid-multivalued-size` value was changed from `{{0}}`/`{{1}}`/`{{2}}` to `{0}`/`{1}`/`{2}` with a `{2,choice,...}` construct. i18next renders all of it literally, so the validation error shown in the admin UI is no longer interpolated.

Lithuanian login message replaced with Italian text

`loginTotpStep1` is now the Italian `Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:` in the Lithuanian login bundle. Lithuanian users will see this sentence on the OTP setup page.

Missing English counterpart crashes the verifier with RuntimeException

The English file path is derived by regex substitution (`resources-community` -> `resources`, `_xx.properties` -> `_en.properties`). If that file does not exist, for example a properties file with no locale suffix or a theme whose English bundle lives elsewhere, a raw RuntimeException is thrown. Because it is not a MojoExecutionException and is not reported as a message, the whole build aborts with an unhelpful stack trace. The missing file should be reported gracefully, or the file should be compared with an empty bundle.

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
rawTokenId null-check validates grantType instead

`Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` checks grantType a second time, so a null rawTokenId is accepted silently. Encoding would then produce IDs like "onrtac:null". It should be `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, ...)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher uses wrong offset and inverted condition, so it never checks the grant

The grant shortcut sits at indices 4–6 of the prefix (e.g. "onrtac"), but the matcher reads `substring(3, 5)`, which gives "ta" for "onrtac". The condition is also inverted: it returns false when the substring *equals* the expected shortcut. Together this means the grant-type check practically always passes. The new assertions in expectCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectDeviceCodeToToken and expectAuthReqIdToToken therefore do not verify which grant produced the token. It should be `if (!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`, ideally with a length check first.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Decoder hard-codes 2-character shortcuts while the SPI contract suggests 3-letter ones

The OAuth2GrantTypeFactory javadoc says the shortcut is "usually like 3-letters", and no length is enforced anywhere. The encoder concatenates whatever shortcut a factory returns, but `getTokenContextFromTokenId` rejects any prefix that is not exactly 6 characters and splits it at fixed 2-char offsets. A custom grant with a 3-letter shortcut will issue tokens whose IDs cannot later be decoded and throw IllegalArgumentException. Either validate that shortcuts are exactly 2 chars at registration and fix the javadoc, or use a delimiter-based format.

true_positives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
testIncorrectGrantType passes because of an NPE, not the intended validation

The factory in this test has a null sessionFactory. An unknown shortcut makes getGrantTypeByShortcut call `sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream(...)`, which throws NullPointerException. Catching `RuntimeException` hides this, so the test never exercises the intended "Unknown value ... for grant type" IllegalArgumentException. It should catch IllegalArgumentException and mock or stub the session factory.

false_positives.candidate:
Lazy refresh of grant maps skips duplicate-shortcut validation

postInit checks that no two grants share a shortcut. The runtime refresh paths in getShortcutByGrantType and getGrantTypeByShortcut just `put` into both maps. A grant deployed later with a colliding shortcut silently overwrites the existing shortcut→grant mapping, so later decoding returns the wrong grant type for tokens issued by the original grant.

Lightweight-token detection now runs for every access token and can NPE without a context client

`initToken` now calls `AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper.getShouldUseLightweightToken(session)` for every access token. That method dereferences `session.getContext().getClient()` without a null check. Before, it was only reached from mapper code. Any code path that creates access tokens while the KeycloakSession context has no client set will now fail with NullPointerException. Consider using `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getClient()` instead.

New abstract getShortcut() breaks existing custom grant type factories

`getShortcut()` is added to the public OAuth2GrantTypeFactory SPI with no default implementation. Existing third-party grant type factories will no longer compile. `initToken` now calls `AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper.getShouldUseLightweightToken(session)` for every access token. That method dereferences `session.getContext().getClient()` without a null check. Before, it was only reached from mapper code. Any code path that creates access tokens while the KeycloakSession context has no client set will now fail with NullPointerException. Consider using `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getClient()` instead.

Lazy refresh of grant maps skips duplicate-shortcut validation

postInit checks that no two grants share a shortcut. The runtime refresh paths in getShortcutByGrantType and getGrantTypeByShortcut just `put` into both maps. A grant deployed later with a colliding shortcut silently overwrites the existing shortcut→grant mapping, so later decoding returns the wrong grant type for tokens issued by the original grant.

true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue point out that adding an abstract `order()` method to the `CryptoProvider` interface will break backward compatibility with existing implementations.

false_positives.candidate:
Removing the multiple-provider error lets equal-order providers be picked silently (FIPS vs non-FIPS)

Before this change, `detectProvider` threw when more than one CryptoProvider was found. Now it sorts by `order()` and takes the first. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return 200.

If two of them end up on the classpath (for example a misconfigured FIPS distribution that also ships the default crypto jar), the stable sort falls back to ServiceLoader/classpath order. One provider is chosen arbitrarily, and the conflict is reported only at debug level. A FIPS deployment could silently run with the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider.

Suggested fix: keep failing (or at least warn loudly) when the top two providers share the same order. Only the lower-priority fallback (the authz-client provider at 100) should be ignored silently.

Test uses a single default-size EC key for ES384/ES512, so P-384/P-521 paths are never exercised

The key pair is generated with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` using the default curve, typically P-256. That same key is used for ES256, ES384 and ES512, so r and s are always about 32 bytes.

Untested paths:
- 48- and 66-byte integers.
- The ES512 case, where the DER sequence exceeds 127 bytes and the long-form length code in `ASN1Encoder.writeLength` and `ASN1Decoder.readLength` is needed.

The test also only round-trips through the custom code. It never checks the DER output with `Signature.verify` or against the BC implementation, so a symmetric bug would pass.

Suggested fix: initialize the generator with the matching curve for each algorithm (secp256r1, secp384r1, secp521r1) and verify the re-encoded DER signature with the JDK.

`len(results) == offset + limit + extra` compares the result count against a value that includes the offset. The slice only returns at most `limit + extra` rows, so for any nonzero offset this branch never triggers.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.

Consequences:
- The last writer wins in the cache, and the other built indexes are simply discarded, wasting work.
- `IndexTenants` and `IndexedKinds` metrics are incremented more than once.
- For file-based indexes, the second `bleve.New(dir)` on the same directory fails (path exists) and the request errors.

Because `TotalDocs` holds no lock, a map write during its iteration is possible. That is a data race, and Go may abort the process with "concurrent map iteration and map write" during startup.

Fix: take `b.cacheMu.RLock()` in `TotalDocs`.

Also, on the error path the function returns `nil, err` without calling `cancel()`, so the cancelable context is leaked. Any goroutines started by a partial init keep running.

false_positives.candidate:
Shared queue pool is shut down on rebalance, so later messages are skipped and committed

`ResultsStrategyFactory` creates one `FixedQueuePool` in `__init__` and passes it to every strategy built by `create_with_partitions`. On a partition revoke, arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the old strategy, and `close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`. That stops all workers and shuts down every queue.

On reassignment, `create_with_partitions` hands the same dead pool to the new strategy (the `assert self.queue_pool is not None` passes). Each `work_queue.put()` then raises `queue.ShutDown`. The broad `except` in `submit()` catches it, logs it, and marks the offset complete.

Result: after the first rebalance, every message is silently dropped and its offset committed, so uptime results are permanently lost. The pool's lifetime should belong to the factory, or each strategy should get its own pool. The tracker state for revoked partitions (`last_committed`, outstanding offsets) should also be cleared.

Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs on its own daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function(...)`, which wraps arroyo's `Commit` callback. That callback is meant to be called from the strategy's `submit`/`poll` on the StreamProcessor thread. It mutates the processor's staged offsets and consumer state without any locking.

Calling it concurrently with the main loop is a data race on the consumer/commit state. It can also fire after the partition was revoked, staging offsets for partitions the consumer no longer owns.

Committable offsets should be computed here, but the actual commit should happen in `poll()` on the main thread.

Unbounded queues, no backpressure

Each `queue.Queue()` is created without `maxsize`, and `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`. The class docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing implements it.

If one group's queue is slow (the exact scenario this PR targets), the consumer keeps pulling messages from Kafka and buffering them in memory without limit. That can lead to OOM, and the outstanding offset sets grow without bound as well.

Use bounded queues and raise `MessageRejected` when a queue, or the total backlog, is full.

Commits stall forever on non-contiguous Kafka offsets

`get_committable_offsets` walks every integer from `last_committed+1` and stops at the first offset not in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed contiguous: transactional control markers and log compaction leave gaps.

When that happens, the missing offset is never added, so the loop breaks there on every pass. Commits for that partition stop permanently and memory grows.

The logic should compute the highest offset below the minimum outstanding offset among those actually seen, rather than requiring every integer to be present.

close() stops committing before draining, and drops queued work

`close()` sets `shutdown_event` and joins the commit thread first, then shuts down the pool. Offsets completed during the drain are therefore never committed.

The pool's `shutdown()` also sets `worker.shutdown = True` before shutting down the queues. Each worker exits its loop after the current item, so the remaining queued items are abandoned rather than drained.

`join(timeout)` ignores its timeout, and the internal joins can block for up to 5s × (1 + num_queues), which may exceed arroyo's join timeout and hold up rebalances. The pool should drain, then do a final commit, then stop.

queue.ShutDown / Queue.shutdown require Python 3.13

`queue.ShutDown` and `Queue.shutdown()` were added in Python 3.13. On any older runtime, the `except queue.ShutDown` clause raises `AttributeError` when evaluated, and `shutdown()` fails (that error is swallowed by the broad except). Confirm the deployed interpreter version, or use a sentinel-based shutdown instead.

The 2009 box model emitted first by the flexbox mixin (`display: -webkit-box` / `-moz-box`) does not distribute auto margins. Browsers that only understand that syntax, which are the reason those prefixes were added, would render the panel immediately after the title rather than at the right edge.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

ActiveModel::Serializers looks for `include_<attr>?` methods. This method is named `include_website_name` with no question mark, so it is dead code and `website_name` is never conditionally excluded.

It should be `include_website_name?`. Even then it would not apply the TL0 restriction unless it also checks `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` or the attribute is declared via `untrusted_attributes`.

Although the golden comment also mentions a minor string concatenation issue, the core problem is clearly matched.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name leaks the hidden website of TL0 users to anonymous viewers

`website` is listed in `untrusted_attributes`, so it is hidden when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` is true (TL0 users seen by anonymous). The new `website_name` attribute is derived from that same website but is not in that list, so it is always serialized.

Anonymous visitors therefore still get the TL0 user's website host and path. The template renders `model.website_name` in that case too, which defeats the anti-spam restriction.

The existing TL0 spec does not catch this because `untrusted_attributes` in the spec was not updated to include `website_name`. Fix: add `website_name` to `untrusted_attributes`.

Sibling-subdomain heuristic treats unrelated hosts under multi-part TLDs as the same domain

For hosts with the same number of labels (more than 2), the code drops only the first label and compares the rest. Examples where unrelated sites compare equal:
- `foo.co.uk` vs `forum.co.uk` (both reduce to `co.uk`)
- `alice.github.io` vs `forum.github.io` (both reduce to `github.io`)

In those cases an unrelated user site gets its full path displayed as if it were same-domain. A public-suffix-aware comparison would avoid this.

`"." << website_host` mutates a string literal

Using `<<` on a string literal mutates it in place. It works today, but it raises `FrozenError` once `frozen_string_literal` is enabled. Use interpolation (`".#{website_host}"`) or `+` instead.

`tempfile.size` may not reflect the file rewritten in place

`Tempfile#size` stats the already-open file descriptor. If the tools replace the file (write a new file and rename it over the path, as ImageOptim does), the descriptor still points at the old inode and reports the original size. Two consequences:
- The loop can keep shrinking the image all 5 times (down to about 33% linear size) even after it already fits.
- `Upload.create_for` receives a stale filesize.

Use `File.size(tempfile.path)` instead. Also note that the result of `downsize` (success or failure) is ignored.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))

`dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)` compares two freshly created object references, so it is always false. A zero-length date override (the way a fixed host marks a whole day unavailable) is therefore never detected as fully blocking. A slot overlapping that instant falls through and is treated as available. Use `.isSame()` or compare `valueOf()`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: using `===` to compare two `dayjs` objects (`dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)`), which compares object references instead of values and always evaluates to false. Both also recommend using `.isSame()` as the fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Working-hours check rejects valid slots when a day has multiple working-hour ranges

`workingHours.find(...)` returns true as soon as any single working-hour entry for that weekday does not contain the slot, and the slot is then rejected. Take a schedule with split hours on one day, e.g. 9–12 and 13–17. A 14:00 slot is outside 9–12, so it is marked unavailable even though it falls inside 13–17. The same happens when one range is split across UTC days.

This check now runs for every fixed host, which includes all users of personal and collective events. Legitimate availability will disappear from booking pages. The check should require that the slot is contained in at least one range (`some` contains), not reject on the first range that doesn't contain it.

Override containment check misses slots extending past override end and slots starting exactly at end

A slot is rejected only if it ends at or before the override start, or starts strictly after the override end.

- A slot starting exactly at the override end passes, because `isAfter` is false when the times are equal.
- A slot that starts inside the override but ends after it also passes.

In round-robin, slots are generated from all hosts' availability. So a fixed host can be booked partly or wholly outside their date override, which is the bug this PR set out to fix. The check should require `slotStart >= overrideStart && slotEnd <= overrideEnd`.

Override day matching mixes timezones and is UTC-date based

The override's day is taken from `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset).format(...)`, which formats in the server's local timezone. The slot's day comes from `slotStartTime.format(...)`, which is in UTC. On non-UTC servers these can disagree.

Matching on UTC dates is also problematic. For organizers far from UTC, an override on local day D can start on UTC day D-1. When that happens:

- Regular slots on UTC day D-1 outside the override are wrongly rejected.
- Day D falls back to normal working hours, ignoring the override.

Offset-shifted override times wrap at midnight and are matched to the wrong day

After applying `offset`, only `hour()`/`minute()` are used, so a shifted override that crosses midnight wraps around. For example, 20:00–23:00 shifted by +3h becomes 23:00–02:00, i.e. startTime 1380 and endTime 120. `buildSlots` skips it because start >= end, so the override vanishes.

Separately, `activeOverrides` (line 207) selects overrides using the unshifted `override.start`. An override that moves into the next or previous invitee day after the offset is still applied to the original day.

Both also suggest replacing `forEach` with `Promise.all(...map(...))`.

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports run eagerly at module load, so nothing is lazily loaded

Each entry is `import("./x")`, not `() => import("./x")`. Every app module starts loading as soon as `@calcom/app-store` is imported, so all ~28 packages (and their dependencies) still load on every cold start. The PR's goal of loading apps on demand is not achieved; only promise wrapping is added.

There is also a reliability problem. If any single app import rejects (bad dependency, missing env at module init), that rejection sits on an un-awaited promise. It surfaces as an unhandled rejection, which can crash the Node process, even when that app is never used.

Use factory functions (`applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) and call them at the use sites.

getCalendarCredentials now returns `calendar` as a Promise and eagerly starts work

`getCalendar` is now async, so `calendar` in each returned item is a `Promise<Calendar | null>`, not a `Calendar`.

`getConnectedCalendars` was updated to await it. Any other consumer of `getCalendarCredentials` / `ReturnType<typeof getCalendarCredentials>` that uses `item.calendar` directly will now call methods on a Promise and break at runtime. This includes API routes and tRPC handlers that list calendars.

Also, these promises are created for every credential up front. If one rejects and the consumer never awaits it, the result is an unhandled rejection.

Either keep the field lazy (store a function) or audit and update all consumers.

try/catch around forEach(async) no longer catches errors

Same issue as in the vital reschedule. The async callback's promise is dropped by `forEach`, so errors from `await getCalendar(...)` and the deletion calls escape the try/catch as unhandled rejections. The deletions also do not complete before the function returns.

Fire-and-forget async forEach in requestReschedule

Recurring deletes pushed to apiDeletes after it is awaited

The outer handler later runs `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` (and `await apiDeletes` on the paid path). By then these pushes have usually not happened, so recurring calendar deletions are not awaited and their errors go unhandled. The new `await getCalendar` makes this ordering race certain.

Use a `for...of` loop, as was done for the non-credentialId branch.

Unhealthy spawn processes are never killed before a replacement starts

The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. Now, when a flusher is detected as hung, the old process keeps running while a new one is spawned for the same shards. Two flushers then work the same Redis shards concurrently, which can produce duplicate or fragmented segments. Leaked processes also pile up on every restart.

`ResultsStrategyFactory` creates one `FixedQueuePool` in `__init__` and passes it to every strategy built by `create_with_partitions`. On a partition revoke, arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the old strategy, and `close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`. That stops all workers and shuts down every queue.

Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs on its own daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function(...)`, which wraps arroyo's `Commit` callback. Calling it concurrently with the main loop is a data race on the consumer/commit state. It can also fire after the partition was revoked, staging offsets for partitions the consumer no longer owns.

Committable offsets should be computed here, but the actual commit should happen in `poll()` on the main thread.

Unbounded queues, no backpressure

Each `queue.Queue()` is created without `maxsize`, and `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`. The class docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing implements it.

If one group's queue is slow (the exact scenario this PR targets), the consumer keeps pulling messages from Kafka and buffering them in memory without limit. That can lead to OOM, and the outstanding offset sets grow without bound as well.

Use bounded queues and raise `MessageRejected` when a queue, or the total backlog, is full.

`get_committable_offsets` walks every integer from `last_committed+1` and stops at the first offset not in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed contiguous: transactional control markers and log compaction leave gaps.

When that happens, the missing offset is never added, so the loop breaks there on every pass. Commits for that partition stop permanently and memory grows.

The logic should compute the highest offset below the minimum outstanding offset among those actually seen, rather than requiring every integer to be present.

close() stops committing before draining, and drops queued work

`close()` sets `shutdown_event` and joins the commit thread first, then shuts down the pool. Offsets completed during the drain are therefore never committed.

The pool's `shutdown()` also sets `worker.shutdown = True` before shutting down the queues. Each worker exits its loop after the current item, so the remaining queued items are abandoned rather than drained.

`join(timeout)` ignores its timeout, and the internal joins can block for up to 5s × (1 + num_queues), which may exceed arroyo's join timeout and hold up rebalances. The pool should drain, then do a final commit, then stop.

This is exactly the scenario the PR is meant to fix. Consider a much shorter TTL for denials, invalidating denial entries when permissions or resources change, or not caching denials for named resources.

`getCachedIdentityPermissions` calls `GetUserIdentifiers`, which falls through to the DB on a cache miss. If that call errors, the error is swallowed and `getIdentityPermissions` immediately calls `GetUserIdentifiers` again, issuing a second identical DB query.

The same happens in List. It is wasted load in the error path, for example when a user is not found.

Remote/cloud client keeps a 30s client-side cache, so the creator issue persists there

Only the in-proc client switches to `NoopCache`. In cloud mode, `newRemoteRBACClient` still caches Check results client-side for 30s.

The server-side re-query on a missing scope never runs for a decision the client already cached. A creator in cloud mode can still be denied access to a dashboard or folder they just created.

This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

`build_integration` then fetches the installation with the app JWT and creates the Integration for whatever `installation_id` was supplied in the query string. An attacker can therefore claim any GitHub installation of the app that has no Integration row yet. Examples:
- an installation whose webhook has not been processed yet (a race);
- an installation whose Sentry Integration was deleted while the app stayed installed on GitHub.

The security validation only covers the case where the webhook already created the row. The installer/permission check should also run on this path, e.g. by verifying the authenticated user can access the installation via `GET /user/installations` with the OAuth token.

The `state` CSRF token is compared to `pipeline.signature` with `!=`, which is not a constant-time comparison. The practical risk is low, but security token comparisons should use `constant_time_compare` (or `hmac.compare_digest`) to avoid timing side channels.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

In non-Dev mode, N requests can arrive while the cache is still empty (for example at startup). All of them see `ret == nil`, queue on `Lock()`, and each in turn reopens and re-parses `assets-manifest.json`, overwriting the cache with a fresh pointer. If the CDN path were enabled, each would also make its own HTTP request while holding the exclusive lock. This adds avoidable I/O and latency, and different callers get different `*EntryPointAssets` instances. Fix: right after `Lock()`, check again `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` (double-checked locking), or use `sync.Once` / `singleflight` for the non-dev path.
